units.title: Unit 17 — Your phone
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 17. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: My phone camera takes clear pictures.
items.note: Here, camera is the device built into a phone. The source index gives /ˈkæmrə/; /ˈkæmərə/ is also heard.

items.example: The message appears on the screen.
items.note: The screen displays pictures, text and other information.

items.example: This app helps me learn new words.
items.note: Short for application; the regular plural is apps.

items.example: I have three language apps on my phone.
items.note: The plural of app; apps are programs you use on a phone.

items.example: Press the power button to turn on the phone.
items.note: A power button turns the phone on or off; a button may be physical or on screen.

items.example: The battery is almost empty.
items.note: A low battery needs charging. Do not confuse the battery with the charger.

items.example: This phone case protects my phone.
items.note: A phone case is a protective cover for a phone.

items.example: I forgot my phone charger at home.
items.note: A charger is used to charge a phone's battery.

items.example: I bought a SIM card when I arrived.
items.note: A SIM card allows a phone to connect to a mobile network.

items.example: My smartphone has a large screen.
items.note: A smartphone combines mobile-phone and computer functions.

items.example: We took a selfie by the sea.
items.note: Use take a selfie, not make a selfie.

items.example: Can we take a selfie together?
items.note: Use take with photos and selfies: take a photo, take a selfie.

items.example: She posts her holiday photos online.
items.note: Post means publish or share content; online tells you where it appears.

items.example: Please answer the phone if it rings.
items.note: Answer the phone means accept an incoming call.

items.pt: correio de voz; mensagem de voz gravada
items.example: I checked my voicemail after work.
items.note: Voicemail can mean the voice-message service or an individual recorded message.

items.pt: deixar uma mensagem no correio de voz
items.example: I left a voicemail when he did not answer.
items.note: Say leave a voicemail, not make a voicemail.

items.example: Text me when you get home.
items.note: As a verb, text can take a direct object: text me. It can also be a noun.

items.pt: enviar algo por mensagem a alguém
items.example: Please text me the address.
items.note: The recipient can follow text directly: text me the address. The words someone and something describe a grammar pattern.

items.example: I got your message this morning.
items.note: A message can be a text message or another short piece of communication.

items.example: I got a message from my sister.
items.note: In this phrase, get means receive.

items.example: You can download the map before the trip.
items.note: Download means transfer digital content onto a device; the verb has final-syllable stress.

items.example: I downloaded an app for train tickets.
items.note: Download an app is a common verb–object combination.

items.example: I call my parents every weekend.
items.note: Call takes a direct object: call someone, not call to someone. Someone is a grammar placeholder.

items.example: I'll call you back after lunch.
items.note: Call back means telephone someone again or return a call. You can say call me back.

items.example: Can you read this message for me?
items.note: Read is spelt the same in the present /riːd/ and the past /red/.

items.example: My phone is locked.
items.note: Locked describes the phone's state; lock is the corresponding verb.

items.example: I always lock my phone at work.
items.note: Lock and unlock are opposite actions.

items.example: Enter your PIN to open the app.
items.note: PIN means personal identification number; it is usually a short security code.

items.example: I can't unlock the screen.
items.note: The prefix un- expresses the opposite action of lock.

items.example: Swipe left to see another picture.
items.note: Swipe is often followed by a direction: left, right, up or down.

items.example: Swipe left to open the menu.
items.note: Swipe left means move a finger towards the left across the screen.

items.example: Swipe right to see the next photo.
items.note: Swipe right means move a finger towards the right across the screen.

items.example: Save your photos before changing phones.
items.note: Save means store information for future use; contrast it with delete.

items.example: I saved the photo in another folder.
items.note: You can save a photo, message or file.

items.example: My phone memory is full.
items.note: In this context, memory refers to the phone's digital storage space.

items.example: The memory is full.
items.note: A phone's memory is full when no more storage space is available.

items.example: Delete the old messages to make space.
items.note: Delete removes digital content; it is not the same as save.

items.example: I deleted a photo by mistake.
items.note: You can also delete messages, files or apps.

items.example: The pictures are in a different folder.
items.note: The exercise uses folder for a place where digital photos are organised.

items.example: They took several selfies on the beach.
items.note: The plural of selfie is selfies. The source uses this form in its phone-use example.

items.example: You can take photos with this phone.
items.note: Say take photos, not make photos; the pattern is reinforced in exercise 17.1.

items.example: My phone has very little memory left.
items.note: Here, memory means space available to store files and messages.

items.example: Put in the PIN to unlock your phone.
items.note: Put in a PIN means enter the security code. This pattern appears in exercise 17.4.

learningObjectives: Identify the main physical and digital parts of a smartphone.
Describe calls, text messages, selfies and app downloads using natural verb patterns.
Give simple instructions for locking, unlocking and swiping a phone screen.
Explain saving and deleting files, full phone memory and everyday phone-use habits.

units.title: Unit 18 — Holidays
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 18. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: We had a relaxing holiday in Wales.
items.note: In British English, holiday can mean time away from work or a trip taken for pleasure.

items.pt: passar férias; ter um período de férias
items.example: We had a wonderful holiday in June.
items.note: Have a lovely holiday! expresses a wish; Did you have a good holiday? asks about an experience.

items.example: My manager is on holiday this week.
items.note: Say on holiday, not in holiday, when someone is away on a break.

items.pt: sair de férias; viajar nas férias
items.example: We're going on holiday next month.
items.note: Go on holiday is a common British English phrase for taking a holiday trip.

items.example: They booked a package holiday to Portugal.
items.note: A package holiday typically includes travel and accommodation in one booking.

items.example: We want a winter holiday in the mountains.
items.note: Winter identifies the season in which the holiday takes place.

items.example: We go camping every summer.
items.note: Say go camping rather than do camping.

items.example: Camping is cheaper than staying in a hotel.
items.note: Camping usually involves sleeping in a tent or another simple outdoor shelter.

items.example: Our tent has room for four people.
items.note: A tent is a portable shelter that people often sleep in when camping.

items.pt: viagem de férias dedicada a caminhadas
items.example: They went on a walking holiday in Scotland.
items.note: A walking holiday is a trip organised mainly around walking or hiking.

items.example: We joined a coach tour of the region.
items.note: A coach is a long-distance bus; a coach tour is an organised trip by coach.

items.example: The plane arrived early.
items.note: Use by plane to say how someone travels.

items.example: We travelled to Ireland by plane.
items.note: Do not use an article after by when describing a means of transport.

items.example: The train leaves at nine.
items.note: Use by train to describe this form of travel.

items.example: She went to the city by train.
items.note: Say by train, not with train.

items.example: We rented a car for the holiday.
items.note: Use by car to describe this form of travel.

items.example: They travelled across France by car.
items.note: Compare by car with on foot when describing how someone travels.

items.example: The ferry crosses the river every hour.
items.note: A ferry carries passengers and sometimes vehicles across water.

items.example: We went to the island by ferry.
items.note: The source contrasts flying with travelling by ferry.

items.example: The coach was comfortable.
items.note: In British English, a coach is generally used for longer journeys than a local bus.

items.example: The students travelled by coach.
items.note: Say by coach to describe transport on a long-distance bus.

items.example: Check your passport before you travel.
items.note: A passport is an official document used for international travel.

items.example: You may need a visa to enter the country.
items.note: Whether you need a visa depends on the destination and your nationality.

items.example: Keep your ticket until the end of the journey.
items.note: A ticket may be for a train, plane, coach or another form of transport.

items.example: I printed our train tickets.
items.note: The regular plural of ticket is tickets.

items.pt: moeda; dinheiro utilizado em um país
items.example: The local currency is different from ours.
items.note: Currency is the money used in a country; it does not mean exactly the same as cash.

items.example: You can pay in the local currency.
items.note: Local currency means the money normally used in the country you are visiting; this phrase is an instructional extension.

items.example: I packed my camera for the trip.
items.note: Here, camera means a device for taking pictures; this word also appears in Unit 17.

items.example: Our luggage is in the hotel.
items.note: Luggage is uncountable: say some luggage, not luggages.

items.example: My suitcase is too heavy.
items.note: Suitcase is countable: one suitcase, two suitcases.

items.example: He carried his clothes in a rucksack.
items.note: Rucksack is a common British English word for a bag carried on the back.

items.example: Are you flying to Spain tomorrow?
items.note: The irregular verb forms are fly, flew, flown.

items.pt: voar para; viajar de avião para
items.example: We're flying to Lisbon on Friday.
items.note: Use to before the destination: fly to Rome. This entry is a verb pattern, not a complete sentence.

items.example: We tried the local food in Greece.
items.note: Try the local food means taste food typical of that area.

items.example: I want to try the local food on our trip.
items.note: Here, try means taste or experience, not attempt to cook.

items.example: This city has exciting nightlife.
items.note: Nightlife includes evening and late-night activities such as clubs and bars.

items.example: We enjoyed the nightlife during our holiday.
items.note: Enjoy normally takes a direct object: enjoy the nightlife.

items.example: Have a great time in London!
items.note: Use this expression to wish someone an enjoyable experience or to describe one.

items.example: I sent a postcard to my grandmother.
items.note: A postcard is a card, often showing a place, sent through the post.

items.example: Please send me a postcard from Rome.
items.note: You can say send someone a postcard or send a postcard to someone.

items.example: The journey was relaxing.
items.note: The transport-comparison exercise uses relaxing for a pleasant, restful journey.

items.example: The coach tickets were cheap.
items.note: The transport-comparison exercise uses cheap to mean low in price.

items.example: Travelling by plane is fast.
items.note: The transport-comparison exercise uses very fast to describe speed.

items.example: Our flight to Madrid leaves at noon.
items.note: The source mentions flights as part of a package holiday; a flight is a journey by air.

items.example: Public transport can be cheaper than driving.
items.note: Here, transport is a noun for ways of travelling from one place to another.

learningObjectives: Talk about holidays using have a holiday, be on holiday and go on holiday.
Distinguish package holidays, camping, walking holidays and coach tours.
Use by plane, by train, by car, by ferry and by coach to describe transport.
Identify documents, money and luggage commonly needed for travel.
Discuss local food, nightlife and sending postcards using everyday travel expressions.
